extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning proof techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Writing and checking elementary mathematical proofs (number theory, parity, divisibility, sets, induction) using standard proof methods and examples as in an introductory proof textbook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose an appropriate proof method
rubrics_metrics.description: Select from direct proof, contrapositive, contradiction, cases, induction, or construction as the situation demands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly labels proofs with the method used (e.g. 'Proof. (Contrapositive)', 'Proof. (Direct)'). Use contrapositive for implications where negation makes the argument easier, contradiction when assuming the opposite yields an immediate impossibility, cases when different parities/remainders lead to distinct analyses, and induction for statements about all natural numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the hypothesis and manipulate definitions/expressions to reach the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical pattern: suppose the antecedent (e.g., a=2n), substitute into the expression, algebraically simplify to show the consequent (e.g., resulting expression has the form 2k or 2k+1). Many examples: proving 'if 14|a then 7|a and 2|a', or subset inclusions by taking arbitrary element and showing membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contrapositive
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove 'if P then Q', show 'if not Q then not P' instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used when negating the conclusion simplifies the argument (e.g., parity statements, irrationality proofs). Remember to apply DeMorgan's law when negating compound disjunctions/conjunctions (demonstrated when proving 'x is even or y is odd' type statements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the opposite of the desired statement and derive a contradiction (often parity or divisibility impossibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: irrationality of sqrt(2) by assuming rational reduced fraction and deducing both numerator and denominator even; showing there do not exist integers a,b with 18a+60b=1 by deriving '1 is even'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Split into exhaustive disjoint cases (often parity or remainder classes) and prove the statement in each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used when variables can be even/odd or have different remainders mod n. Several proofs enumerate cases 1–3 for parity combinations of a and b; ensure coverage of all possibilities and explain why cases are exhaustive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent integers by parity forms
rubrics_metrics.description: When dealing with parity, write integers as 2k (even) or 2k+1 (odd) to deduce parity of expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used throughout: e.g., show a^2 odd implies a odd by assuming a=2k+1 etc., compute expansions (2k+1)^2 and simplify to 2(…) +1. Also used for higher powers with similar expansion logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use modular/remainder reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason about divisibility and residues by working mod n or analyzing remainders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: show 4 does not divide n^2 + 2 by considering n mod 2; use mod 3 reasoning in proofs about 3|a^3 implying 3|a; use modular residues to rule out integer solutions to Diophantine equations (sum of squares mod 4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisibility proofs by exhibiting integer multiple
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove 'm | t', exhibit integer k with t = m·k (or deduce existence via algebraic manipulation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical steps: from a | b deduce b = a·d; substitute into expressions and factor to show divisibility of related quantities (e.g., gcd and division-algorithm proofs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Congruence (mod n) manipulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Preserve congruence under addition, multiplication, and powering to prove congruence statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: show a = b (mod n) implies a^2 = b^2 (mod n) by expanding a^2 - b^2 = (a-b)(a+b) and factoring out n; show transitivity of congruence by using divisibility definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: GCD equalities via mutual divisibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove gcd identities by showing each gcd divides the other (or by showing each is both a common divisor and maximal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: gcd(a,b)=gcd(a-b,b) proven by showing any common divisor of a and b divides a-b and vice versa; often proceed by letting d = gcd(a,b) and showing d divides r, and conversely letting e = gcd(r,b) and showing e divides a.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the division algorithm in gcd proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply a = q b + r and then show gcd(a,b) = gcd(r,b) by divisibility arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard technique: express a and b in terms of d = gcd(a,b), deduce r is multiple of d, and then reverse the argument for gcd(r,b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving irrationality via reduced fraction contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume number is rational as reduced fraction a/b, use arithmetic to derive that a and b share a nontrivial common factor, contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic examples: sqrt(2) and cube roots; show a^2 even implies a even, leading to both a and b even; for cube roots use mod 3 divisibility argument that if 3|a^3 then 3|a.

rubrics_metrics.name: Providing counterexamples to disprove statements
rubrics_metrics.description: To refute a universal claim, present a specific counterexample and verify it violates the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: disproving |x+y| = |x|+|y| with x=1,y=-1; disproofs in the exercises list follow this pattern—select simple numeric examples and compute to show failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical induction structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove base case (usually n=1) then assume statement for k and prove for k+1 by algebraic manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sum formulas like 1+2+...+n = n(n+1)/2 and sum of cubes; show base case, then add (k+1) and simplify using algebra to reach formula for k+1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving if-and-only-if statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish both directions: (=>) and (<=), choosing direct, contrapositive, or cases as convenient for each direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'a + b even iff a and b have same parity' — prove one direction with contrapositive and the other by cases (both even or both odd).

rubrics_metrics.name: Element-wise set proofs (mutual inclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove set equality A = B show A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A by taking an arbitrary element and using definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: proving distributive laws, DeMorgan identities, or equality of constructed integer sets {12a+4b} = {4c}; show membership both ways and produce the witnessing integer when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cartesian product proofs via coordinate membership
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove inclusions/equalities of product sets by taking an ordered pair (a,b) and reasoning about membership of a and b in component sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for statements like (A×B) ∪ (C×D) ⊆ (A∪C)×(B∪D) by checking both cases (in A×B or C×D) and deducing a∈A∪C, b∈B∪D.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic factorization to deduce divisibility or compositeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Factor polynomials or expressions to show a nontrivial factorization (hence divisibility or compositeness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: showing 2^ab -1 factors as (2^a -1)(...), proving that if 2^n -1 is prime then n must be prime by factoring when n = ab; using (x-1) factor to show f(b+1) composite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parity/odd-even behavior of powers and signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit that even powers are nonnegative and preserve evenness, odd powers preserve sign/parity in arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: when x<0 odd-power terms are negative and even-power terms are positive, used in sign comparisons; odd powers of integers preserve oddness in parity arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting multiples for divisibility of product sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Argue that among k consecutive integers there are guaranteed multiples of certain primes, so product divisible by their product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: product of five consecutive integers is multiple of 5·4·3·2 = 120 because the block contains a multiple of each of 5,4,3 and at least two multiples of 2 (or alternatively use binomial coefficient divisibility argument).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use DeMorgan and logical equivalences when negating compound statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Negations of conjunctions/disjunctions are handled by DeMorgan's laws; needed in contrapositive/contradiction proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: negating 'x is even or y is odd' gives 'x is not even and y is not odd' (i.e., x odd and y even), which then guides case expansions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show uniqueness or impossibility by parity/counting contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Derive contradictions like '1 is even' or '0 is odd' to refute assumptions about existence or parity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: assume an equation holds and manipulate to produce absurd parity (1 even) or impossible equality, which disproves the assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Bezout identity when gcd = 1
rubrics_metrics.description: When gcd(a,b)=1, use that ax + by = 1 for some integers x,y to deduce divisibility consequences (e.g., a | bc ⇒ a | c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: multiply ax+by=1 by c and substitute bc = a·z to show a divides c.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove subset relations with nonempty set hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving A×B ⊆ A×C implies B ⊆ C, require A nonempty and use an arbitrary fixed element of A to reduce to coordinate membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if A ≠ ∅ choose a∈A; then (a,b)∈A×B and inclusion gives (a,b)∈A×C, hence b∈C. Explicitly note nonemptiness assumption.
